title: Epistulae imperatorum pontificum aliorum
author: Papal letters
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0045a.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: cum per omnia ex integro ageret, suspexit et Athanasius ut ueri uindicis atque in Graecum stilum transtulit, ne tantum boni Graeca lingua non haberet. parum est: quin etiam propriis litteris idem Athanasius eosdem libros praedicat ut prophetarum et euangeliorum atque apostolorum doctrinis et pia confessione contextos. et quamuis plurimis in eum laudibus erigatur, tamen non aequat ad meriti eius praeconium. et quidem cum amplius laudare non posset: ita rerum eius supereminentia quaeuis laudans lingua superatur.
passages.english: Since he dealt with everything thoroughly, Athanasius too looked up to him as a defender of the truth and translated [his work] into Greek, so that the Greek language should not lack so great a good. That is not all: the same Athanasius also, in his own letters, proclaims these same books as woven together from the teachings of the prophets, the gospels and the apostles and from a pious confession. And although he is raised up by very many praises of him, still he does not match the proclamation of his merit. And indeed since he could not praise [him] further: so greatly is any tongue that praises surpassed by the pre-eminence of his achievements.
passages.notes: The passage is syntactically awkward: 'erigatur' (passive, 'is raised up') seems to refer to the praised author, while 'aequat' has Athanasius as subject. The sentence beginning 'et quidem cum amplius laudare non posset' appears incomplete or loosely joined to what follows. The author praised is not named in the passage; he is probably Hilary of Poitiers, but this cannot be confirmed from the text.

passages.original: quod si, ut ceteri auctores haereseos, qui iam dudum ab apostolica sede uel a patribus iudicati et extra sinum matris catholicae ecclesiae effecti perpetua morte perierunt, etiam hi, qui nunc deprehensi sunt uel deprehenduntur, in perfidia sua permanent, spiritali gladio, quo interimantur, tradantur: ut nunc Pelagius Caelestiusque, qui a beatae memoriae praecessore tuae beatitudinis papa Innocentio, si rectam respuant fidem et in sua peruersa doctrina perdurent, damnati sunt.
passages.english: But if, like the other authors of heresy, who long ago were judged by the apostolic see or by the fathers and, cast out of the bosom of mother catholic church, perished by perpetual death, these also who have now been detected or are being detected persist in their faithlessness, let them be handed over to the spiritual sword, by which they may be slain: as now Pelagius and Caelestius, who were condemned by your Beatitude's predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Innocent, if they should reject the right faith and persist in their perverse doctrine.
passages.notes: The syntax is loose: 'etiam hi... permanent' serves as the protasis after 'ut ceteri', and the final clause ('ut nunc Pelagius... damnati sunt') is elliptical. The conditional 'si... perdurent' qualifies the condemnation by Innocent, so the condemnation applies only if they persist.

passages.original: adicitur etiam in eodem capitulo. quia sic a Christo Christiani uocemur, quomodo diuersarum sectarum uel errorum sequaces ab inuentoribus et magistris suis sunt sortiti uocabula, id est ut a Platone Platonici et a Marcione Marcionistae et a Manichaeo Manichaei. si quis igitur haec ita sapit docet credit aut praedicat, anathema sit. nos enim ideo Christiani uocamur et sumus, quia ipsum dominum nostrum Iesum Christum baptisma percipientes induimus et ipso nobis existente capite omnes in eodem unum corpus efficimur.
passages.english: It is also added in the same chapter: that we are called Christians from Christ in the same way that followers of various sects or errors have received their names from their founders and teachers, that is, Platonists from Plato, Marcionists from Marcion, and Manichaeans from Mani. If anyone therefore so thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things, let him be anathema. For we are called Christians, and are [Christians], for this reason: that receiving baptism we have put on our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and with him as our head we all become one body in him.

passages.original: Iuuenalis reuerentissimus Hierosolymitanus episcopus dixit: (Qui conuertuntur, scriptura diuina suscipi iubet. quapropter et ab haereticis reuertentes suscipimus. unde peruideo reuerentissimum Ibam mereri clementiam, quia et senex est et ut habeat episcopatus gradum, catholicum existentem\'.
passages.english: Juvenal, the most reverend bishop of Jerusalem, said: 'Divine Scripture commands that those who turn back be received. Therefore we also receive those returning from the heretics. Hence I judge that the most reverend Ibas deserves clemency, since he is both an old man and [deserves] to hold the rank of bishop, being catholic.'
passages.notes: The closing quotation mark is garbled in the edition ('\''). The final clause is elliptical.

passages.original: nam et uenerabilis memoriae Iuuenalis interlocutio hoc idem significat: quod Ibas episcopus de id, quod sancto Cyrillo capitula eius aliter intellegendo detraxerat, postea professus, quia his ab eo explanatis et a se intellectis in communionem eius deuote concurrerit et de his, quae prius aliter intellexerat.
passages.english: For the interlocution of Juvenal of venerable memory also signifies this same thing: that Bishop Ibas, regarding the fact that he had disparaged Saint Cyril's chapters by understanding them otherwise, afterwards professed that, once these had been explained by him and understood by himself, he had devoutly come into communion with him, and concerning the things which he had formerly understood otherwise,
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; it continues in the following passage ('had been converted...'). 'de id' is ungrammatical Latin and is probably a scribal or edition error for 'de eo'.

passages.original: Lupercalia autem propter quid instituta sunt, quantum ad ipsius superstitionis commenta respectat, Liuius in secunda decade loquitur nec propter morbos inhibendos instituta commemorat sed propter sterilitatem, ut ei uidetur, mulierum, quae tunc acciderat, exigendam. proinde si uel ad hoc ipsum aliquid hoc ualeret, hoc intermisso non morbus acciderit, contra quem Lupercalia reperta non sunt.
passages.english: As for why the Lupercalia were instituted, so far as concerns the inventions of that superstition itself, Livy speaks of it in his second decade. He records that they were instituted not to check diseases but, as it seems to him, to drive out a barrenness of women which had occurred at that time. Accordingly, even if this had any power for that very purpose, when it was discontinued it would not be disease that befell, against which the Lupercalia were not devised.

passages.original: . unde libellum cum litteris misimus, cui uos subscriptiones proprias < oportet > inserere, ut fides uestra, quam directa per Rufinum diaconem scripta testantur, apud nos fiat huius quoque repetitionis adiectione manifestior. Data XVII. Kal. Decembr. Petro cons.
passages.english: Therefore we have sent a document together with the letter, to which you must add your own signatures. In this way your faith, which the writings sent through the deacon Rufinus attest, may become more manifest to us by the addition of this repetition as well. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Peter.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. 'oportet' is the editor's supplement. The seventeenth day before the Kalends of December is 15 November.

passages.original: sicut enim uidetur ambiguum dicere simpliciter (upum de trinitate) non praemisso nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi, sic eius personam in trinitate cum patris spiritusque sancti personis esse non dubitamus. sine Christi ia namque persona nec credi trinitas religiose potest nec adorari fideliter, quemadmodum sanctus Augustinus ait: an aliqua ex trinit.ate persona, et alio loco: solus in trinitate corpus accepit, et iterum: unus us trium.
passages.english: For just as it seems ambiguous to say simply 'one of the Trinity' without first putting the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, so we do not doubt that his person is in the Trinity together with the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit. For without the person of Christ the Trinity can neither be religiously believed nor faithfully adored, as Saint Augustine says: 'one person of the Trinity'; and in another place: 'he alone in the Trinity took a body'; and again: 'one of the three.'
passages.notes: There are scanning errors: 'upum' for 'unum', 'ia namque' (possibly 'iam namque'), 'trinit.ate', and 'unus us trium'. The first Augustine quotation, 'an aliqua', is corrupt and probably reads 'una aliqua' ('one person'). The last, 'unus us trium', is perhaps 'unus ex tribus'.
